screens.body:
WebAssembly (WASM) is a way to run code in the browser at near-native speed. Instead of JavaScript, you compile languages like Rust, C++, or Go into a compact binary the browser executes fast.

It doesn't replace JavaScript — it sits beside it. JS handles the UI; WASM handles the heavy lifting.

options: Near-native-speed code running in the browser
check.question: WebAssembly is…

screens.heading: Code at near-native speed, in the browser
screens.keyPoint: JS for UI, WASM for heavy lifting.

screens.body:
Why bother? Some work is just too heavy for JavaScript: video editing in the browser, 3D games, photo editors like Figma, scientific simulations. WASM makes those possible without plugins or installs.

If your app ever feels slow doing math on big data, WASM is the tool to reach for.
screens.heading: Why WASM exists
screens.keyPoint: Heavy compute in the browser, no plugins.

screens.body:
A runtime is the environment that executes your code. Node.js let JavaScript escape the browser and run on servers — that's the runtime you know.

Now there are modern challengers: Deno (from Node's own creator, secure by default, TypeScript built in) and Bun (blazing fast, all-in-one runtime + bundler + package manager).

options: The environment executing your code — Node, Deno, Bun
check.question: A runtime is…

screens.heading: Runtimes: beyond Node
screens.keyPoint: Node was first; Deno and Bun are the fast newcomers.

screens.body:
What does a runtime actually give you? Two things: an engine that runs your language, and APIs to touch the real world — files, network, timers, environment variables.

Browsers give JS the DOM; Node gives it the filesystem. Same language, different superpowers depending on the runtime.

options: An engine to run code + APIs to reach the system
check.question: A runtime provides…

screens.heading: What a runtime does
screens.keyPoint: Engine + system APIs = your code can do things.

screens.body:
The newest trend: edge runtimes. Platforms like Cloudflare Workers and Deno Deploy run your JavaScript in data centers all over the world, automatically picking the one closest to each user.

Your API responds in 20ms instead of 200ms because the code runs in Calgary, not Virginia. Same code, closer execution.

options: Your code runs in the data center nearest each user
check.question: Edge runtimes…

screens.heading: Code that runs next door
screens.keyPoint: Closest data center wins the latency race.

screens.body:
When should you care about any of this? When you hit real limits: startup time too slow (Bun boots fast), security defaults matter (Deno denies file access unless allowed), or global users complain about lag (edge runtimes).

Don't chase new runtimes for fun. Chase them when you can name the problem they solve.

options: Only when you can name the problem it solves
check.question: When to adopt a new runtime:

screens.heading: When to care
screens.keyPoint: Name the problem first, then pick the tool.

screens.body:
Trying them is cheap: WASM via a library like ffmpeg.wasm in a web page, Bun with a one-line install, Deno Deploy with a free tier. An afternoon experiment teaches more than a week of articles.

That's the habit this whole course builds: small, time-boxed experiments with new tech.

options: A cheap afternoon experiment beats a week of articles
check.question: How to learn a new runtime:

screens.heading: Try it in an afternoon
